en: Having meditated upon the goddess Śruti, the embodiment of sacred learning— who is like an ocean of the nectar of the jewels of hymns—
Lakṣmaṇa, who has recited a hundred thousand hymns, composed this compendium of sūktas in honor of Sarasvatī. (1)
Now, the praise of the Jina:
May that Jina, the son of Nābhi, protect us—
he who, with his golden-hued body, cast himself into the fierce fire of asceticism for the sake of purification.

May that Lord of Jinas be for our prosperity— he in whom the sun of absolute knowledge (kevalajñāna) perpetually rises, even when devoid of passion (aparāga), which is a marvel indeed. May that divine Jina be victorious in the salt-ocean of saṃsāra.
May the son of Nabhi protect you— he by whose blazing austerity the submarine fire was eclipsed; in whose mirror of absolute knowledge even all things,
though formless and obscured, shine forth clearly.
May the sight of the illustrious Vṛṣabha be for your auspiciousness— he who,
though born of a cow devoted to the Brahmins, brought forth the Supreme Bull.
He is like the hair of those with sin, which obstructs the tenth gate [the anus].
May that Victorious One (Jina), the hero who uprooted [Māra], protect you all.
Now, regarding Hara: may that Śiva, with whom Gaurī is ever united in body, protect you eternally.
Embraced by her, he shines like a golden creeper upon a silver tree.
May that Śiva protect you forever—
he over whose head the three cities whirl like a waving lamp-offering (ārātrika) ignited by the fire of his arrow.
May the throat of the blue-throated Lord protect you— dark as the *tamāla* tree,
serving as a golden touchstone for the arms of the ever-embracing Pārvatī.
May the throat of the blue-throated Lord, resembling a dark rain-cloud, protect you.
May that mass of matted hair of Dhūrjaṭi bring you victory, wherein the arm-creeper of Gaurī shines like a streak of lightning;
and wherein even today the Jāhnavī creates the illusion of a single grey hair.
Victorious is Dhūrjaṭi, who bears a mass of matted locks, from whom sprouts the crescent of the rising moon,
and who is the seed of the origin of all that moves and is stationary.
The cool-rayed moon is fixed upon his head, and Pārvatī is immersed within his body.
May that enemy of Smara purify you—he who, in battle, was like the weapon of Smara himself.
May that Śiva grant you auspiciousness, upon whose head the formidable matted locks display the playful charm of a garland of moss served by the waters of the Gaṅgā. 7–8. 15.

May the form of the Great Lord—possessing the elephant-faced moon as his joy, yet being the joy of the elephant-faced moon himself; burning away the bodiless Cupid, yet possessing arms that bear the serpent—be for your delight.
May he who holds the syllables of flattering spells at his throat and the water-pot of her breasts in his hand [grant you bliss].
Oh, how wonderful is the unbroken vow of the Lord of Pārvatī!
Having placed a pair of gourd fruits upon her breast like two breasts, Pārvatī appears as if she intends to express the unfathomable depths of Śambhu’s mind.
May He protect you ever auspiciously, wherein Brahmā and the other gods emerge and perish like bubbles in the great ocean of phenomenal existence. 12. 19.
Now, Hari—

May the lotus-navel of Hari grant you perpetual prosperity— that lotus upon which the Creator, humming the syllable Om, acts like a honey-gathering bee. May that Hari protect you, by whom, while binding Bali, [the earth was raised].
Having made themselves small, the gods were led to greatness.
Victorious are the hands of Narasiṃha, with their shimmering tips of claws,
as if marked by fragments of the crescent moon drawn out in anger from the deer-marked one.
May that Vāmana protect you, in whose reflection within the Kaustubha gem the three worlds appeared as if they were his own belly, gazing upon him with curiosity.
May he protect you, [he] who is radiant with the beautiful leaf-designs transferred from the cheeks of Lakṣmī.
May the arms of Śauri protect you— arms that bear fruit everlastingly through their dense shade.
May the circle of the snout of Hari in his Boar incarnation be victorious,
upon whose tusk the splendor of the earth’s mark shone like a crescent moon.
May the chest of Viṣṇu, resplendent with the Kaustubha gem, nourish your prosperity—
seeming as if it had been sealed by Śrī herself to prevent Rādhā from entering.
May those [arms] of his, dark as rain clouds and hardened by the striking of the Śārṅga bowstring, protect you.
The four arms of Hari are the pillars of the pavilion of the three worlds.
Now, the poet [describes] the bow of the poet Śrī Vāmadeva, who is like the god of love.
Neither speech nor the five-arrowed god (Kāma) has failed to take root in whose mind?
(1) Both the lords of poets and the lords of elephants, moving with a gait slow with rut, desire to dwell either in the forest or in the palace of the sovereign of the earth. (2)
How can we praise that poet, the illustrious Kālidāsa,
by whose three poems even a mortal becomes a wise deity?
(3) The sages do not know how to praise the single poet, the illustrious Vālmīki.
How can he who has no second at all be considered the foremost poet?
(4.31) The very same arrangement of words, the very same rows of syllables—yet in the mouth of one person after another, there is a certain cleverness here and there. (5.32)
6. With their bodies covered in horripilation from tasting the flavor of well-spoken verses, poets dwell in happiness even without the company of a beloved woman. 33.
It is fitting that poets have been surpassed in their placement of words by Murāri.
In the past, even with its three steps, this [mountain] did not overstep the three worlds. May that mountain—the source of the river of nectar-like prose—born from Subandhu, be victorious;
for by encountering its poetic breaks and wordplays (*bhaṅga-śleṣa*), poets have themselves encountered their own literary failures (*bhaṅga*).
Some possess unimpaired eloquence, while others have their brilliance impaired;
some are like lamps inside jars, and others merely follow the literal text.
Poets such as Kālidāsa and others are poets, and we too are poets.
The status of being a category (padārtha) is established both for "I" and for an atom.
(10) The pride of poets surely vanished because of the *Vāsavadattā*, just as that of the sons of Pāṇḍu vanished when Śakti came within the range of Karṇa. (11)
Even his breath does not issue forth while Bāṇa dwells within his heart;
how much less so his speech, with its elaborate flourishes and rhythmic compositions?
There are those who possess the status of their caste in every house, as numerous as dogs.
There are not many poets who are creators [of works], like *sarabha* deer;
how could those lords of poets, whose eloquence flows from their mouths without weariness even at the end of a chapter (*ucchvāsa*), not be worthy of homage? (13–14)
Now, as for poetry:
Fortune, though she takes the form of gold, rests only upon the hands and feet;
but the Goddess of Speech, though her form consists of mere syllables, adorns the inner self. (1.42)
There is a certain unprecedented aesthetic flavor (rasa) in the fruit of poetry, arising from the excellent creeper of well-spoken verses;
though its relishing is common to all, the person who truly savors its sweetness is rare.
O Sarasvatī, this unprecedented treasury of eloquent sayings is seen in you.
What is imperishable undergoes decay, and what is perishable spreads far and wide. (3) 44.
Water, food, and well-spoken words—these three are the jewels upon the earth;
yet by the foolish, the designation "jewel" has been applied to mere fragments of stone. (4) 45.

Blessed are they, those great-souled ones, whose fame remains steadfast in the world—those by whom poems have been composed, and those who are celebrated within the poems. (5) 46 Those who understand [the truth] are seized by envy; those in power are defiled by pride.
And others, struck by ignorance, let well-spoken words wither away within their own bodies.
(6) What is the use of that poet’s poetry, or what is the use of the arrow of the archer, if it does not strike the heart of another and cause his head to reel? (7)
What more need be said of that poetry which, merely upon being heard, does not cause the faces and heads of enemies to hang down? Now,
as for the good man:
Oh, how truly wonderful are the deeds of the great-souled!
They regard fortune as a mere blade of grass, yet they bow down under its weight.
When a terrible calamity, harsh in its nature, falls upon them by the decree of fate— || 1 || 50 ||
For the minds of the great are indeed armored with fortitude by means of the thunderbolt.
(2.51) Affections that last until death, angers that vanish in an instant, and renunciations free from attachment—these arise among the high-souled. (3.52)
For men of lofty mind, these two things bring happiness:
either the renunciation of all attachments or vast and extensive prosperity.
Like a cluster of flowers, the conduct of the wise man is twofold.
Either they shall stand at the head of the entire world, or they shall perish in the forest alone.
Those of unrestrained mind do not set foot upon anything insignificant,
for their desires remain boundless even when they have attained the whole world.

For one who is modest, of noble birth, and desiring to beg for wealth, his speech flutters back and forth in his throat like that of a pigeon. (7) At first slender, then broad-waisted, they expand at every step. (56)
The friendships of the virtuous, like rivers, flow onward and never turn back.
O high-souled one, do not despair because the dull-witted do not uplift you;
for only elephants are capable of pulling out elephants sunk in the mud.
The joys of all embodied beings imitate a shallow bowl:
they hang downward for the wicked, but in the opposite way for the wise. Now, as for the villain:

How indeed does that wicked, evil-mouthed, and loquacious sinner continue to live, when not even a drop of nectar remains in his mouth? (1) What rivalry can there possibly be between a wicked person and a self-respecting man of noble character? (60)
For whom speaking terrifyingly and reviling the virtuous is an ornament.
(2) 61 Having fashioned the tips of the tongues of the wicked—which take away the lives of all men—did the Creator make weapons, poisons, and fires in vain? (3) 62
Thorns pierce with a single point the foot of a single person;
but the wicked, with a thousand mouths from afar, take away the lives of all.
(4) There are only two ways to deal with both the wicked and thorns.
Either by breaking his sandals or by avoiding him from afar,
a virtuous person, even while living, is unable to act in such a way as a wicked person, once dead, might do harm to men. (64–65)
Even the sweet words spoken by the wicked produce terror in us, like untimely blossoms.
A master who is greedy, stubborn, dishonest, foolish, and utterly cruel— [is not to be served].
"Indeed, this wicked man will die after having caused many virtuous people to perish.
(8) How could that slanderer not be equal to the tail of a dog, which, though possessing crookedness, reveals its very secret? (9)
Beauty for the sake of another's wife, wealth for the sake of tormenting the world, and power for the destruction of the virtuous— such are the most wicked qualities found in the villain.
These certain unprecedented villains truly cause wonder in our minds.
For those with whom no connection to sesame seeds is ever seen. (11) Ah! Truly, the serpent-like villain possesses some unprecedented method of slaughter:
he clings to the ear of one, yet another is deprived of life. (12)
Even when made clear by affection and the gift of prosperity, a wicked person—
and likewise a mirror standing nearby— renders even a single thing into two.
Envy dwells within a base person like a hidden treasure.
How indeed can that wretched and wicked man attain humility, when his face is seen to be sealed shut whenever others are praised,
and when depravity dwells within him from head to foot?
For one who is rigid by nature yet assumes a feigned bow,
even a virtue leads to the injury of others— just as it does for a bow and a wicked man. First they reveal themselves, and thereafter they produce blindness.

The meanings of the words of the wicked are like the flash of lightning; they exist for a moment and then vanish. (17) Even instruction given to the wicked leads only to provocation, not to tranquility;
drinking milk for serpents serves only to increase their venom. (18)
Even when treated with honor, a wicked person provokes quarrels among the virtuous;
does a crow ever attain the state of a swan, even if washed in milk?
(19) A boat and the tongue of a wicked person both move in a contrary direction.
By whom was this cruel thing created solely for the purpose of deceiving people?
(20) Even at the end of life, a wicked person remains wicked;
the *indravāruṇī* gourd does not attain sweetness even when fully ripe. (21cd)
How can he who is deceived by his own tongue not be deceived by others, when he speaks while deceiving his own mind?
Alas! The mind of the wicked, possessed of crooked intellects, is difficult to grasp.
One thing is in their speech, another in their throat, and another resides in the cavity of their lips.

(23cd) For those for whom the slaughter of living beings is a sport, whose words pierce the vital organs, and whose duty is to cause suffering to others—they are the death even of Death itself. (24cd)
For rogues who subsist merely on the knowledge of how to harm others, the accumulation of virtues is only for the sake of their snare, like that of slaves. 25.
Now, the poetic challenge (samasyā):
For two young lovers standing on a deserted street amidst the heat of the fierce summer season,
finding joy in their conversation with one another, even the sun acts like the moon. (1.85) In some places the constellation Mṛgaśiras is dense, and in others the Kṛttikās hang down.
In some places, the sky, filled with falling rain, acts like the dwelling of a hunter.
O beloved, there is a certain new smoke-bannered fire of passion within your heart,
whose downward-pointing wick of incense is the line of hair upon your body.
The Puruṣa of a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet— O Lord, he creeps away, crushed, terrified, and hidden by your army.
(88ab-88cd) [Of the Master of Knowledge.]
"During this quarrel, there will be an equality between me and one who is not my equal"—
thinking thus, the proud lion surely flees from the deer.
[This occurs] during the rainy season, when the beloved has uttered words that are dear yet life-destroying.
Marked by the crow-like lightning—the messenger of her beloved’s arrival—she is perceived everywhere:
in all directions, upon the earth, on the mountain, and in the sky.
When her life is in peril, that slender woman becomes like Nārāyaṇa himself as she is remembered.
For those who are intoxicated by their learning and yet exhibit miserliness despite possessing wealth— upon whom the curse of fate has fallen, fire has arisen from the water.
May there be well-being for the king, the god of the kṣatriyas, the god of the world.
If the sky within your fame-lotuses acts like a bee,
look at the difference in greatness: the earth, along with its oceans and mountains,
shines like a female bee upon the lotus-garland of the hoods of the serpent Śeṣa.
Like a guarantor for a meeting, the moon forcibly delivers the lover who has been hidden within the cave of darkness to Kāma;
[this occurs] when his mind is overwhelmed by the blow of Dāmodara’s hand.
And the wrestler Cāṇūra beheld the sky as if it were covered with a hundred moons.
Gradually, he will make the sky appear white as camphor, the moon pink like coral,
and the collyrium white as milk.
From Rāghava, who drew his bow to his ear in longing for union with Sītā,
a cloud of dust rose from the ocean like the embers of his arrows;
he whose beloved stands afar, fresh and with full breasts.
Neither a pond nor clouds can quench his fever;
"Come! Go! Fall! Rise! Speak!
Observe silence!"—who has not been made to do these things by her whose eyes are like those of a startled deer? (99cd–100)
If indeed that which is inside this body were to become outside,
then that slender-limbed woman would be visible externally without any effort at all.
Va, vā, avi, vi, vu, vū, ve, vai, vo, vau, vaṃ, va— such are the vowels.
When the soldiers set fire to the city, the tears of the enemy women began to flow.
Then the king attained equality with you; neither the Moon nor the Sun [is your equal].
The hand of that donor never tires, neither by night nor by day. O King, poverty quickly abandons him whom your affectionate glance favors for even a moment, as if out of jealousy.

O Lord of Fortune and Fame, we do not know who will cease their toil while you, the Creator, continue to produce the poor and bring others to the fulfillment of their goals. O King, the row of lotuses upon the blade of your sword shines resplendently.
The row of syllables [of your fame] appears as if inscribed by the marks of the scratches made by your enemies summoned at the hour of death.
(4) 106cd These seven oceans, resembling drinking-vessels, are the cage for the royal swan of your fame throughout the three worlds. (5) 107ab–107cd
"You are all-possessing and all-giving"—thus you are falsely praised by the wise.
Enemies have never gained your back, nor have the wives of others gained your chest. (6) 108.
Generally, people are required to perform penance for engaging in forbidden sexual intercourse.
His fame reaches even the inaccessible and is honored everywhere. (7) 109.
To this extent, that protector of heaven remedies doubt;
for he does not reproach himself as a paramour who caused the fall of Ahalyā. (8) 110.
By the slender woman who is steaming with heat and shedding tears from her eyes,
the rivers dry up while those on the slopes of the Vindhya mountains flourish;
the quarters of the sky resound with a crackling noise and the heavens turn crimson.
When his elephant-force moves along, the vermilion on the ears of the elephants is scattered;
for Chittapa, who always alone faces three fears from many enemies simultaneously, [this is a source of joy].
"O King, that you give away what you do not possess is a great marvel.
By Hari, the earth was lifted up by assuming the form of a boar;
but by you, O King, it has been done without becoming a boar—this is a great marvel."
It is a marvel that the cause is seen in one place and the effect in another:
the majesty of Your Lordship is great, yet the burning of Your enemies occurs within their own hearts.
There is no counting Your faults or Your virtues; they are beyond measure in You.

Because his virtues are immeasurable and because no faults exist in him, [he remains supreme]. || 14 || 116 On the field of battle, he simultaneously drew out the life-force from the bows and from the hosts of enemies, both of whom were born of royal lineages. || 15 || 117
When his vanguard, with Indra [the wielder of the thunderbolt] as its leader, advances, the vital breaths of his rival kings seem to flee away in emulation. (16) 118.
By Someśvara.
I believe that the bow of your enemies must have remained fixed within their very hearts;
otherwise, how could it have bent down upon them on this field of battle? (17) — Vāhaḍa.
Generally, those who are perishing perceive everything as contrary to reality;
for even you, though as golden-hued as gold, have become the very death of your enemies.
Having ascended the scale, the sun has placed its foot upon Scorpio.
It has been placed upon your head by the serpent-chiefs without any effort at all.
How could Dharma wander on this single foot during this Kali age,
were it not for your lineage to serve as its support?
"May your parting lines not be marked by vermilion, lest you become women;
may your enemies depart far from your borders, leaving their swords behind.
"What is the use of that which does not contain you? And where you are, can there be this Kali age?"
If your birth is in the Kali age, then let it be Kali; what is the use of the Kṛta age?
(22) If thorns are seen nowhere else but upon the stalks of lotuses and the bodies of lustful men, it is because you are protecting them. (23)
Your fame, as if born benumbed by its previous immersion in the ocean,
has gone to the orb of the sun to seek warmth, O Lord of the World.
From where have you learned this unprecedented science of archery?
The flood of supplicants approaches, while his virtue departs to the ends of the earth.
(25) Upon the pillar of his arm, the row of calluses from the bowstring shone;
I imagine it to be an iron chain for the elephant of victory. (26)
His bracelet mercilessly crushed the thorns, for he could not tolerate even a drop that was superior to himself. (27) Recalling his strung bow, his adversaries [were struck with fear]. (129)
Even the mere sight of his creeper-like eyebrows caused the womenfolk to tremble with longing.
(28) Granted that the moon may rival him by the name of "King" (Rājā), how could it possibly possess sixteen digits multiplied fourfold? (29)
In Pṛthūdaka, at the Śatapuṣkara sword-site,
even when merely seen, the heap of sins of sinful men is destroyed.
Let the enemies fall there, having never tasted the pleasures of life.
Like the breasts of noble women consumed by the fire of youthful widowhood,
O Lord, you have acted like Nārāyaṇa, the enemy of Naraka,
in that not even a single Śiśupāla has been left remaining among the race of your foes.
In this Kali age, you alone have accomplished the securing of the next world by means of pure arrows that follow upon your virtues and have been made effective.
O King, you alone are the foundation of Pātāla; you are the binding support of the quarters.
And you alone are the source of the breezes from the *cāmara* fans for the three worlds.
(136cd) The sun, whose orb is momentarily eclipsed [by Rāhu], who torments all creatures with his sharp rays that are difficult to behold—such a one as he is not equal to you. (137ab–137cd)
Sarasvatī resides in your mouth, and Lakṣmī resides in your palace;
O King, has Fame become angry that she has gone to another land?
How can there be well-being in the family of those who are at odds with you?
Their dwelling shall also be restricted to the forest, which is filled with the practice of skillful means (kuśalatā).
Due to their hostility toward you, their enemies have adopted the Buddhist view (saugatadarśana):
that all things are momentary in nature during conflict, and that there is emptiness (śūnyatā) in all objects.

The sound of his trumpeting causes agitation in the waters of the Gaṅgā, as if he were bathing, though he is burdened by the sin of causing the miscarriage of the offspring of the water-wives. Then he became calm.
In dream there is a deficiency of the aspect of consciousness, while in waking there is the grasping of objects.
The wise say that the state which transcends both dreaming and waking is the supreme goal.
He who, having pierced through the shell of the cosmic egg, does not proceed to that which is higher than the highest—[is not liberated].
How can that person, while still dwelling in the womb, receive the designation "man"?
(2.143cd) Let alone old age, death, misfortune, and disease;
I consider even birth itself to be repeatedly a source of shame for the wise man. (3.144ab–144cd)
Make your dwelling either in the waters of the Gaṅgā, which wash away all sin,
or in the captivating, pearl-encrusted pair of breasts of that slender-limbed woman;
whether in the heat of summer with the *puṭapāka* [sweat] or in the rainy season with the downpour of water.

In the winter, all people are constantly afflicted by cold fevers. (5) 146 Even hair, which is perpetually borne upon the head and nourished with oils, becomes discolored; what else does not undergo transformation? (6) 147
Having touched a corpse, one attains purity by bathing with one's clothes on;
yet for one who increases his own [sin] by that very act, how can there be purification? What is not already sufficient in this case—namely, the total avoidance of meat?

For one whose mind is disciplined, even a blade of grass causes their own body to ache. (8) 149 What logic is there in maintaining this body—whose ultimate end is such that it becomes worms, ashes, or excrement—by inflicting suffering upon others? (9) 150

For one who constantly practices purification and performs the libations to the ancestors, if the mind is not agitated, what can the scripture do for him? (10) When your intellect crosses beyond the thicket of delusion, [then you will attain peace]. (151)

Then you will attain detachment from that which remains to be heard and that which has not yet been heard. (11) Even kings serve [the senses], they enjoy sense-objects, and they take delight with women—alas, what audacity these men possess! (12)
She who,
out of love for her husband, gives herself to one who is unkind—
even though she has no affection for herself— who indeed would consider her to be truly enamored? (13.154)
That Creator first created four means;
he did not create even a fifth by which women might be restrained. (14) 155.

Neither by pride nor by generosity, neither by honesty nor by service, neither by weapons nor by scriptures—by no means whatsoever can anything be achieved against women. Oh, hunter! You are truly greedy; why do you ask [others] again and again?
She who sees does not speak; she who speaks does not see.
(16) Treasures abide in his presence, the wish-fulfilling cow follows him, and the gods act as his servants—he for whom contentment is his ornament. (17)
To the knower of Brahman, heaven is as a blade of grass; to the hero, life is as a blade of grass;
to the dispassionate man, a woman is as a blade of grass; and to the desireless man, a king is as a blade of grass.
(18) This very Prayāga is proclaimed as the gateway to liberation. (159)
Where the Gaṅgā and Yamunā flow on both sides of the Goddess, bestowing their splendor—
this Prayāga is the most exalted of all sacred fords (tīrthas). From this place,
the further shore of saṃsāra is beheld by those who remain here.
This is that banyan tree named Śyāma; even its shade is resorted to by those dwelling there as a supreme light, owing to the miraculous deeds of this [sage].
O dear one, the deer in the forest are praiseworthy, for they subsist on a diet of dūrvā grass and the tips of kuśa shoots.
Those whose minds are intoxicated by worldly existence do not see their own faces.
(22) 163 The ocean was bound with stones, Indra was conquered by men, and Laṅkā was besieged by monkeys; why is all this not seen by those who still live? (23) 164
Why is this supreme great sin not declared as the sixth—that which is manifested by a multitude of evil desires at the gateway of the Lord?
Truly, sensual pleasures are enchanting; truly, worldly prosperities are delightful.
But life is indeed as flickering as the sidelong glances of an intoxicated woman.
(25) Life has exhalation as its limit; that exhalation is but the wind.
There is nothing more unstable than the wind; that one lives at all is a marvel. (26)
All accumulations end in depletion; all elevations end in a fall; unions end in separation, for life indeed ends in death. Day by day, death draws closer to every living being.

Like a condemned man being led to his execution, he suffers vexation at every step. For the sake of this tiny body— a repository of all impurities, ungrateful, and perishable— fools commit sinful deeds.
When impermanence first embraces a newborn as if it were a nurse, what room is there for grief later, when even a mother cannot protect him?
(30) He who rules the earth bounded by the oceans as if it were a single city—
She has but a single belly; why then do you praise her sovereignty?
It would be better to touch two venomous serpents—bulging, coiled, and having just cast off their skins—than to touch the breasts of that slender woman.
In childhood one is composed of father and mother; in youth, of the woman;
in old age, of one's progeny; the deluded person is never composed of the Self at any time.
In this beginningless cycle of existence, where the god whose banner is the sea-monster is difficult to resist—
What doubt can there be regarding one's lineage, which is rooted in desire, or regarding wealth?
(34) How can those men, devoted to sin, sleep at night, when their calamities in the hells are separated from them only by death? (35)
Lack of restraint over the senses is said to be the path to calamities;
their conquest is the path to prosperity. Go by whichever way you please.
(36) [The body] has bones for its pillars, is bound together by tendons, and is plastered with flesh and blood.
Abandon this abode of living beings, strewn with urine and excrement.
It is my conviction that he who is tranquil in the early stage of life is truly tranquil;
for when the bodily constituents are wasting away, in whom does tranquility not arise?
If you, O mind, fix your delight upon that very object, in that very place, and in that very manner, you shall not be a vessel for suffering. 39. 180.
Now, the praise of women.
"My beloved does exactly what pleases me"—he knows this, yet he does not realize that she performs it only for his own pleasure.
What other method could there be than the noose of a lover's arms? || 1 || 181 ||
When placed around the neck it gives life; when cast away it kills.
(2) 182 This necklace rolls upon the circle of breasts of fawn-eyed women; such is the condition even of pearls—what then of us, the servants of Love? (3) 183
Having bound only a single Bali, Hari attained greatness;
likewise, even though the slender woman possesses the three folds [of skin], that same curvature remains in her waist.
Only one Bali was bound by Viṣṇu after he had assumed a dwarf form.

O slender one, I believe that the three folds of your waist were bound by you with mere playfulness. (185cd) I praise those beautiful-eyed women who, with their very glance, restore to life the Mind-born God whom he had burnt with his gaze—those who triumph over the Three-Eyed One. (186)
"There has never been, nor is there now, nor will there ever be a woman equal to her"—
with this desire, the Creator drew three lines upon her for the sake of her triple folds (trivalī).

Where there is no wisdom, how can there be knowledge? Where there is no Dharma, how can there be compassion? (386cd) Prosperity quickly attends one who provides for the future, who is vigilant, who is free from anger, who begins tasks early, and who is not despondent. (387)

Trade is for those who think "I have wealth"; agriculture is for those who think "I have something"; service is for those who think "I have nothing"; and daring is for those who think "I am not [bound by anything]. When well-advised, well-executed, well-performed, and well-considered— (388–389ab)
For those who have resolved upon an undertaking at its inception, success is unfailing.
By that Creator, while fashioning the four means of attainment in the beginning,
no fifth was created by which women might be restrained.

They speak with one man, they look with amorous glances at another, and they think of yet another within their hearts; indeed, who truly is the beloved of women? That which is in their inner mind is not on their tongue, and that which is on their tongue is not what is outwardly shown.
Women of diverse conduct do not do outside what they do within. One should either not enter an assembly or speak what is improper;
for by either remaining silent or speaking falsely, a man becomes guilty of sin.
Even the father of one who has set out while standing at a distance becomes angry;
he [the father] follows the path of his younger brother, even if he is emaciated—let this remain so.
Now, as for the wretched man...

In a man, a woman who is defiled by intimacy with another is nothing but a mockery; what beauty could she possess? It is like fashioning a bracelet upon a withered arm. Begging is the ultimate embodiment of poverty, not merely a smallness of wealth.
Śambhu, though the Supreme Lord, possesses wealth in the form of an old bull;
yet, like a miserly corpse that is already dead, he gives nothing.
By increasing his own flesh, he has only rendered a service to the crows.
A miser who possesses noble conduct is superior to one who is generous but lacks it;
for the former gives his wealth when asked, while the latter gives even his life, and thus his life is more than his wealth.
This was because in the past, he had practiced two syllables: "na," "asti" (it is not). (398–399ab)
This very thing—"Give! Give!"—has presented itself in a perverse form.
A hoarse voice in the throat, paleness in the face, and trembling:
these which are the signs of death are the very signs of the beggar.
To what refuge have they gone that they are being destroyed like poison? (401ab) Why are riches neither abandoned nor enjoyed by the miser?
(401cd) There has never been, nor will there ever be, a donor equal to the miser. (402ab)
If we become wealthy through wealth that is devoid of both giving and enjoyment— wealth that one bestows upon others without even touching it oneself—
are we not truly wealthy by means of that very wealth? (402cd–403)

If that wealth of men were barren of both giving and enjoyment, and were not enjoyed by friends—what indeed would be considered misfortune? He who, having rendered a service, desires a return favor from that person... [404–405ab]
Wretched because he is subject to craving, he licks up even what has been vomited.
Whatever you give to the Brahmins and whatever you eat day after day—that, I consider, is your wealth; the rest you merely guard for someone else.
Now as for fate:
having placed the fetters of a wife upon him, the Lord of Creatures was not satisfied;
he bound him further with the neck-chain of offspring.
"What was not to be, does not come to be; what is to be, cannot be otherwise.
Why is this medicine, which destroys the poison of anxiety, not drunk?
Those who exist at dawn do not exist at midday; those who exist at midday do not exist at night.
Those things which exist in the night do not exist on other days; oh, what a magical illusion of Fate!
Having carefully examined noble lineage, learning, age, valor, and good character, Fate—the skillful one—bestows poverty just as it bestows a daughter.
Fate is not the master only among men; it is the master even among the gods.
While the Lord of Wealth was his friend, Hara remained clothed only in skins. Fie on fate! Though his eyes were clear, they became vessels for the ash of collyrium.
A golden vessel with a hole and a crooked middle;
bees, grey with pollen, drink the honey within the lotuses, while swans eat the moss—fie on this inconsistent fate! 412cd–413ab / 7cd–7ef.
"Alas, father! Even though it is contrary to our interests, do not treat these two pairs with the same regard as you do the virtuous:
servitude toward one who lacks discernment, and affection for a person devoted to another.
"There is no way whatsoever by which that destiny might not come to pass for one who is unworthy."
Just as one's own shadow can never be overtaken by living beings,
what will scholarship, modesty, or even valor avail?
For when fate seeks out one's vulnerabilities, it renders all virtues fruitless.
Now, concerning medicine:
travel is old age for humans; lack of travel is old age for elephants.
Abstinence from sexual union is old age for women; sexual union is old age for horses.
Ātreya says that food should be eaten only when one is hungry; Kapila says compassion toward living beings;
Bṛhaspati says lack of trust; Pāñcāla says gentleness toward women.
That which is not eaten by day, and that which is not eaten by night—[these are the views of others]. (418ab–419ab)
That which is not eaten when one is hungry causes living beings to decay;
cold weather, long journeys, poor food, women whose youth has passed,
and opposition to the mind— these are the five causes of old age.

In some places it is warm, in some cold, and in some it is boiled and then cooled; in some places it is mixed with medicine, yet water is never prohibited anywhere. Sunlight is pungent and dry, while shade is sweet and cool.
Moonlight is astringent and sweet, and darkness removes all defects.
One suffering from colic should avoid split pulses; one with skin diseases should avoid meat; one with fever should avoid ghee;
one with diarrhea should avoid fresh food; and one with eye disease should avoid sexual intercourse.
Flour is eight times more nourishing than grain; milk is eight times more nourishing than flour;
meat is eight times more nourishing than milk; and ghee is eight times more nourishing than meat.
Physical exercise destroys phlegm (kapha), and massage destroys wind (vāta).
Then one should perform this triad, including bathing, for the destruction of bile.
"O Mother, thereafter you shall have five sons, O Hero; of this there is no doubt."
Whether Karna remains with Arjuna slain, or whether I remain with Arjuna slain— behold Dhananjaya, O Karna, who is as difficult to gaze upon as the sun, as difficult to cross as the ocean,
and as difficult to comprehend as the meaning of the Vedas.
While I am alive, that my father should suffer the seizing of his hair—
how could others, having sons, ever envy those who have sons?
The three Vedas are at the tip of my tongue, and the bow with its arrow is in the palm of my hand.

There was fear for Droṇa from both [his son and his pupil], from the curse as well as from the arrow; for even though he had been adopted by Kauśika, such fear arose due to the succession of his kinsmen. Even for Triśaṅku, neither heaven nor earth was available for his enjoyment.
A noble steed does not endure the stroke of a whip, nor a lion the roar of thunder; likewise, those who possess great vigor cannot tolerate being pointed at by others with a finger.
For the low-minded, [authority] rests on the tips of their tongues, while for the wise, it resides in their hearts.

Anger dwells within heroes, who have extensively engaged in their duties. What is the use of those poems, strengths, or riches, by which one has not become a yogi as a listener, nor an enemy like unto a god, nor a seeker of wealth equal to oneself? (432cd–433)

If one who gives, one who fights, or one who recites does not experience horripilation, then shame on his giving, his prowess, and his speech—both for himself and for others. When honored, he extends his hand; when victorious, his bow is drawn into a circle.
If he acts again in this manner before me, shame on his generosity and shame on his prowess!
Many men here, though crippled, study the science of weapons;
those who can endure the falling edge of an enemy’s sword are rare indeed.
For those who have resolve as their companion, neither the peak of Mount Meru is too high, nor the depths of Rasātala too low, nor the ocean too boundless.
Do not fear; these are not swords possessing the luster of blue lotus petals.
These are the playful glances from the eyes of Śrī Avalokinī.
By breaking the bow— which was composed of all the gods and invincible to all kings—
Rāmabhadra has conquered the two worlds.
Whether it be the elder brother, the ten-necked Rāvaṇa, or the younger brother, Vibhīṣaṇa—
whom will the hero consecrate, according to the method of positive and negative concomitance?
Now, the miscellaneous verses (prakīrṇaka):
Scorched by the midday sun, the elephant plunges into the lake,
eager to uproot the lotuses that belong to the Sun-god from their midst—
[lotuses] which possess thorns at their tips, unpleasant shadows, roughness, and crooked natures.
The desert land, with its karīra trees produced from the forest-king (the *vānaspatya*), undergoes a transformation:
that which is a virtue of crystal becomes a defect;
for by its transparency, it reflects the shadow even of those who are powerful.
Alas! That you were entreated and praised under the mistaken impression that you were a *cintāmaṇi* jewel—all that, O stone of a verse, must be forgiven by us who are but supplicants.
A palm tree that begins to grow tall perishes along with that very state of rigidity.
Whether a rain of embers falls or a violent wind blows,
may you either remain hairless or grant the most immediate fruit;
even by such procrastination, O palm tree, the forests of the virtuous [will suffer].

The sandalwood tree, whose sole essence is fragrance, is served even when it is fruitless; likewise, even serpents serve [the tree] without food—such is the nature of destiny. By those very trees with their masses of fresh leaves that the tree was nurtured, [it is now served].

That he casts away those very things that have grown old— what is so strange about one of base birth? That the earth holds little value for a mere fragment of stone is the manifestation of a brilliance whose essence has not yet set.

The very same men who have reaped, humiliated, and trampled the rice now nourish those very same ones when they are distressed; how can there be such a perversion regarding what grows from one's own field?
O slave, if this jujube tree belonging to a slave-girl pleases you, [then take it].
For what more need be said? Are these grapevines not a direct fountain of nectar?

Alas, where have those trees of the mind gone—those which were so rich in sprouts and flowers, so abundant in the excellence of their blossoms and fruits, and so prolific in the growth of their fruit-bearing shoots? 451cd–452cd.
Since the determination of its multitude of qualities depends upon fragments of stone,
why was that gold not simply melted away right there in the belly of the fire? It would have been well indeed if the Creator had not needlessly exerted himself in its formation.
What is the use of the fruit of sandalwood, which does not correspond to its own nature?
By me, greedy for jujube fruits and ignorant of trees,
a khadira tree was sought in the forest because of its resemblance to thorns.
Either it becomes a great tree or it perishes along with its roots;
the sprout of the *nyagrodha* seedling does not undergo an intermediate developmental stage, [yet it provides] leaves, flowers, fruit, shade, roots, bark, and wood. (456ab–457ab)
Blessed are those trees from whom seekers depart without having obtained their desires;
possessing shade, free from predatory beasts, with noble growth, and yielding fruit—
such great trees on the roadside exist solely for the welfare of others.
Indeed, for those who have no recourse, even suffering does not arise from humiliation;
for the most part, *aśoka* trees put forth new sprouts when struck by feet.
They are pierced or entered according to whatever condition one desires.
What kind of purity can there be for that dull object consisting of crystal?
In the desert there is no water at all; even if some is obtained with great difficulty, it is bitter, scanty, and hot, and does not bring about the end of thirst.
Having abandoned his own son Krauñca and his father Himālaya,
what has been achieved by this [Garuda] who entered the ocean merely to protect his wings?
Even the fruit of the cotton plant, though devoid of sap, is pleasing to us.
The birth of those who consist of virtue is for the protection of the secrets of others.
A son does not hate his father by nature, because he is born from his own seed.
One should know that the son who hates his father is one begotten by another's seed.
When you have sons born to you and remember even a little of the affection we showed toward you, then you will understand.
For as he is being born, he takes away his wife; as he grows, he takes away one's wealth.
One who is dying may take away one's life; there is no enemy equal to a son.

(466cd) The best are renowned for their own virtues; the middling are known through their father and mother; the low are known through their maternal uncles; and the lowest of the low are known through their fathers-in-law. (467)
"Child, that which was not studied by you during those nights spent with fawn-eyed women—
that is why, though a learned man, you sink like a cow in the mud amidst the wise.
By carrying out the commands of your parents while they live, and by providing abundant food on the anniversary of their death..."
In the shade of a tree and from the alms-bowl—by these three alone is one truly a son.
What has been accomplished by that son who, as a thief of his mother’s youth, neither dug ponds nor planted trees? (469cd–470)
Between two sons born of the deer species, it is better for a father than one who is unborn, dead, or a fool;
for those two cause but little grief to their parents, whereas a fool causes great grief.
There is nothing greater than the birth and death of a son for the experience of happiness and sorrow.

There is nothing greater than the killing of a Brahmin for sins, nor than the horse-sacrifice for merits. Therefore, my dear son, act in such a way that you may always behold yourself adorned with those various distinctions in the mirror of the interior of the three worlds.
Of what use is he who is born, merely robbing his mother of her youth, if he does not rise to the pinnacle of his lineage like a banner? Now, the jests of her friends:

"Since he was not won over by conciliation or bribery, even though dissension was shown— well indeed that punishment was inflicted by me upon the ill-behaved one! Your lower lip is devoid of passion, yet those eyes of yours are full of impurity."
"O messenger, your throat is a monastery; have you become a female renunciant?
By this lower lip of yours, which is like a Buddha free from passion, the emptiness of all things has been declared without guile. (476cd–477)
"Why do you conceal your breasts and your face with your hand, O messenger?
Only those whose lower lips and breasts have been bitten by a lover shine beautifully.
"O messenger, what is the use of that wicked man who transgresses the scriptures?"
"Five five-nailed animals are fit to be eaten, yet you have been eaten by a sixth!
With both your sides struck by powerful blows and your lower lip mangled by wounds,
O messenger, you are fit for battle, not fit for the work of a messenger."
"O messenger, you must forgive the wounds from my nails and teeth when I am emaciated;
eighteen akṣauhiṇī divisions have perished for the sake of my friend.
O messenger, that deed which you have performed is difficult for anyone else to accomplish."

One who destroys those who have sought refuge, seeking out vulnerabilities, has been torn asunder. Your body is emaciated, your gait is weary, the pupils in your eyes are rolling, your speech is indistinct, and your garment is loose; O messenger, why are you feverish?
What need is there for much speaking here, O messenger? For the sake of accomplishing my purpose, even my own flesh was given; what then to say of other things?
— Vararuci.
Then it was clearly true that she was Pārvatī and he was Sthāṇu;
even though they were joined together, they remained free from desire for the full enjoyment of sexual union.
He might be a pillar, or he might be a goat, or perhaps he is the Lord of Beasts—
he who utterly consumed the flower-armed god, the teacher of amorous dalliance for women.
Whatever a beautiful-browed woman performs with her amorous gestures toward lovers, [he alone can surpass].
All of that falls upon the hips alone, even though they are innocent.
By the very same fragment of cloth with which the sun travels by day, the moon travels by night; oh, the poverty of these two!
Between a jester and a scholar, the jester is better than the scholar;
for even the jester wins a hundred thousand coins, while the scholar departs humiliated.
Between a crow and a beggar, the crow is better than the beggar.

Even a crow receives a morsel of food, yet a beggar does not receive even a single morsel. Kṛṣṇa played with cows; how wonderful! The goddess Lakṣmī, though fickle by nature, is truly devoted to her husband among those who regard him as equal to cattle. || 490cd–491 ||
The *ketakī* flowers are strewn with thorns, and lotus plants arise from the mud; where is there a jewel that is free from affliction?
[Just as] while the scribe remained in his mother’s womb, fearing he was her prey... 492–493ab.

The intestines were not eaten; therein lies the cause for his toothlessness. Having taken the initial syllables from "greediness from the crow," "cruelty from Yama," and "firm striking from the carpenter," by whom was the *kāyastha* created?
Fortune favors those Bhaṭṭas and Cāraṇas who perform the division of words without hiatus for Sarasvatī. Now begins the section on flattery (cāṭu).
Even though you go far away, you do not leave my heart,
like the shadow at the close of day that clings to the base of a forest tree before it.
This lower lip of yours, with its luster like coral, is like a desert path.
O charming girl, whose mind would it not agitate with thirst?
497cd Even though your gaze is devoted to Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, it hangs upon Karṇa; O sweet-voiced one, who could place such excessive trust in you? 498ab–498cd
"O woman of shapely hips, it can be determined that you possess a waist;
otherwise, the existence of the weight of your breasts would be impossible.
O charming girl, what kind of unprecedented archery is seen here in you?"
By which you pierce hearts with virtues alone, and not with arrows.
Well done, young girl! Your breast-mound has been made far outward;
I know what kind of pain it inflicts when it is submerged within the heart.
O slender-limbed one, your breasts are hard though you are delicate; O fair-faced one, they are full yet have a cruel aspect.
For this very reason, your two breasts have moved outside of your heart.
When your servant has fallen at your feet, why does your hand remain upon your face?
"O wrathful one, who will remove my anger when I am afflicted by desire? Now, as for virtues:
a great difference is observed between those who possess virtues and those who are devoid of them. (503cd–504ab)
The necklaces upon the throats of women and the anklets upon their feet—
those pearls which have found a place upon the weight of their breasts act only as the virtues of threads whose gaps have been concealed.
"O brother, do not show disregard for virtues, even if you possess great fortune;
for a jar, though completely full, falls down into the well when its rope is severed.
One attains height through virtues, not by sitting upon a high seat. (506–507ab)
Does a crow perched upon the pinnacle of a palace act like Garuḍa?
(507cd) Generosity is the virtue of the wealthy; wealth is the virtue of the generous. But when wealth and generosity are separated from one another, they are a mere mockery. (508)

One devoid of virtue does not recognize the virtuous, while one possessed of virtue is envious of those who possess it. Rare indeed is the person who is both virtuous and devoted to virtue, and straightforward.
Even a spider falls downward from the very web of its own virtues.
Withdrawing that very [activity], he attains the supreme state on high.
Without the wheel, the manifestation of qualities leads only to downfall;
regarding this, the spider serves as the illustration for those who hold contrary views.
Now, whatever is difficult to reach, whatever is difficult to accomplish, and whatever is situated far away—
all that can be achieved through austerity; for austerity is indeed difficult to surpass.
Having previously conquered the senses, you conquered the three worlds;
yet now, as if remembering that enmity, you have been conquered by those very senses.
One should not place trust in the senses, even when they are absorbed in fierce asceticism.
Viśvāmitra also embraced Menakā with longing.
Having practiced the "five-fire" penance in summer, staying in the open air during the rains,
and sleeping in water during the winter, he performed most rigorous austerities.
Having become one with a smooth belly, he should protect his hands and feet with his eyes;
he should guard his eyes and ears with his mind, and his mind and speech with his actions.
This servant endured the afflictions of cold, wind, and heat, as well as other hardships.
Even by performing austerity for a thousandth part of that [time], one might become happy.
How can those who have neither learned sons nor abundant wealth attend upon the *agnihotra* like an elephant in rut?
Then, those ascetics, who were pure from former lives and had reached the state of full maturity,
continued to enjoy the fruits of their own austerities.
Now, knowledge should be acquired with all one's being by the wise even when advanced in age;
for that which is easily obtained here may not yield its fruit in another birth.
By whom is the face of the sciences not kissed, just as that of courtesans? Yet, those men who capture their very hearts are rare indeed.
Now, regarding illusion (māyā):
The difficulty of [logical] consistency is an ornament of ignorance, not a defect;
for if it were possible to establish it in any way at all, it would no longer be ignorance.
This duality is mere illusion (māyāmātra); from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha), there is non-duality (advaita).
The entire world is in a state of liberation; delusion is the cause of bondage.
Now, as for craving—this bottomless pit of craving is difficult to fill; by whom can it be filled? (523cd–524ab)
That which is dug up even by great efforts through repeated fillings;
the face is overcome by wrinkles, the head is marked by grey hair,
the limbs grow slack, yet craving alone remains youthful.
Surely its internal essence emerges along with the state of being sought;
otherwise, for that which remains in such a condition, by what cause could there be lightness?
That a dead thing attains heaviness—this has now been understood by me.
The desire for lightness is the root [of this practice], for that [desire] ceases once one has died.
Then, the noble one [performs it] by standing with one foot below and the other above.
The distinction between the giver and the beggar is indicated by their very hands:
though their poverty is equal, the dispositions of their minds are diverse;
some grieve that they have not given, while others grieve that they have not received.
Blessed are those who, having their desires fulfilled by the mere perception of a form, do not hear the piteous words of suppliants;
for even the generous and the seekers themselves cry out, "Give! Give! (530–531).
They do not perceive anywhere with impetuosity whether [something] exists or does not exist.
Alas, what great misery! Even one who possesses sight begs;
it is more fitting for the blind man to beg than for one whose face has never been seen to do so.
Reddened by the saffron from the swelling breasts of Lakṣmī,
that very hand of Hari by which Bali was made a mere recipient for alms— [that hand] is now the sun.
Now, the sun:
The rising of the sun alone is praiseworthy; what is the use of the rising of others?
For when he has risen, there are neither darknesses nor [other] lights.
Of what use is the age of those born with brilliance, once that [sun] has appeared?
Even the rays of the youthful sun fall upon the mountain peaks;
as if out of satisfaction with its thousand rays, it obtains even more than desired.
What further need is there for others, even if they are well-pleased, who possess only two or four rays?

O Sun, we do not know what you will do when you are no longer impartial, since even while standing in the middle, you destroy this shadow of the world. [Just as] by the sun, who is like a twice-born man leaning toward the southern quarter...
By this, not only has he made himself insignificant, but the very day as well. A firefly shines only so long as the moon does not rise;
but once the thousand-rayed sun has risen, there is neither firefly nor moon.
The sun rises red and sets red as well;
in prosperity and in adversity, the great remain uniform in nature.
Now, the lake:
"Friend, ask the elephant how deep or how shallow the lake is:
standing on the bank, the goat drinks the lotus-free water with its knees.
Long ago, the ocean was drunk by a single person, the jar-born Agastya."
But this lake cannot be emptied even by ten million of his ancestors.
Furthermore, O dear one, deer in the forest that subsist on sprouts of durva grass and kusha grass are worthy of praise. (542d–543ab)
Those whose minds are intoxicated by worldly existence do not see their own faces.
543cd The doe stands still and boundless when the deer is fixed in its trap—she is as if immortal yet breathless, with her inner longing stilled and her wounds healed. 544ab–544cd
Now, for the wealthy, there is hatred for those who serve them and affection for the dull-witted; it is only natural that they should disregard their elders.
Like those suffering from fever, the wealthy always have a bitter taste in their mouths.
Embraced by others, they stumble even on level ground;
the wealthy speak indistinctly, like drunkards.
"Come! Go! Fall! Rise! Speak! Observe silence!"—thus do they command.
In this way, the wealthy play with supplicants who are seized by the crocodile of hope.
A wise man should take refuge in a lord who possesses these five qualities: being sought after, generosity, independence, and knowledge of what is appropriate. (547cd–548)

Generally, in this world, the thirst for wealth is most intense among the wealthy. Behold: a bow made of excellent bamboo, though it possesses two ends (koṭi), bows down even before a single hundred-thousand mark (lakṣa).
Even when the gain of two ends is at hand, the bow born of a noble lineage remains bent.
But Śara, being of low lineage, remained stiff with the apprehension of failing to hit the mark;
yet even that glance of his, which was fickle by nature and fell even upon impurity, his servants highly esteemed as that of their master. (550cd–551)
Homage to those objects that create a sense of distinctness even among brothers who have shared a single womb, been nourished by a single stream of milk, and lived together from birth.
Now, [he becomes] poor.

For a pauper who is destitute of virtue, wealth, and pleasure, and who subsists on the food of others, a long life is as useless as that of a crow. O Poverty, salutations to you; by your grace, I have attained my goal.
"By means of which I behold the world, yet no one beholds me. Then, the pair:
"These two persons in the world pierce the solar orb."
A wandering mendicant devoted to yoga and one who is slain facing the enemy in battle—
these two men abide above heaven in this world. A lord endowed with forgiveness and a poor man who is generous— these two also abide above heaven.
These two should be cast into the water with a stone tied tightly around their necks:
a wealthy man who does not give, and a poor man who is a mere ascetic.
These two men in this world act solely on the basis of others' trust: [557–558ab]
Women desire what they have desired; the world honors those who have been honored.
These two men in the world are never happy:
he who, being poor, desires [wealth], and he who, being powerless, becomes angry.
These two types of persons do not exist in the world now, nor will they exist in the future:
he who does what is requested [of him], and he who does not request anything from another.
These two types of men cause headache for all the worlds: [he who is asked] and [he who asks].

A householder without worldly undertakings, and an ascetic with possessions—this is the experience of one's own self: "To the one whose nature is infinite pure consciousness, unconditioned by space, time, and the like. (561cd–562ab)

Salutations to the peaceful radiance, whose sole authority is one's own direct experience. We offer our salutations with joy to that Self, which shines by its own light and upon which the waters, the earth, and the sky depend for their very existence.

I bow to that Experience, which is unborn, immeasurable, infinite, and whose very form is the bliss of the Self; she is the variegated wall for the painting of the world, beginning with the Great Principle (mahat).
There is a vast difference between the sweetness of sugarcane, milk, and other such substances.

Nevertheless, even Sarasvatī herself would be unable to describe the difference between these two. This world is like the night for both the crow and the owl; as for that which is night for all beings, Hari himself has declared it so.
Now, in spring,
having bathed in a reservoir after touching a flowering creeper,
the wind blows very gently, as if apprehensive of contact with her once more.

At night, breezes blow that are friends to amorous women exhausted by lovemaking; they are perfumed by the fragrance of jasmine flowers from the swaying braids of beautiful women. Under the pretext of being *kiṃśuka* trees, they climb upon the trees on all sides.
The fire seems to look upon the forests as both burnt and unburnt;
that women should seek refuge with their beloved of their own accord is the behavior of the cuckoo,
blinded by the intoxication of spring.
The cuckoo on the tip of the mango tree, tawny with the pollen of flower-clusters, becomes manifest through its cries, just as a man of noble birth is revealed by his actions.
This swarm of bees, sweet-voiced with intoxication, is not crying out; it is merely humming.
This is the sound of the bow of Kandarpa being drawn.
(572cd) The lotus stalks from within the water have bristled with joy;
they seem to have risen up to hear the sweet song of the cuckoo. (573ab–573cd)
The bee, thrilled by its first union, kisses the mango blossom after embracing it,
just as a lover kisses his beloved; meanwhile,
the female cuckoo, not seeing her mate in the forest, has been searching for him for a long time.
Having entered the fire of the red aśoka tree after crying out many times, she perished.
Now follows summer:
the cuckoo, though its throat is parched, dwells within the udumbara tree that has burst into fruit.
